candidates.attacker_control: A content author controls the link target text of a wiki-syntax link (e.g. XWiki 2.1 '[[label>>target]]'), the target of a typed/untyped image or link reference, or the href attribute of an <a> element in XHTML/HTML content that is parsed by this library (via the HTML/XHTML parsers and the annotated XHTML round trip used by the editor). Both the URL-type path (target matching 'scheme://') and the interwiki path (target with '@unknownAlias') are fully attacker-controlled strings.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: I checked for any scheme allow-list or deny-list in the repository: search_code for 'javascript', 'getScheme', 'scheme', 'startsWith("http', 'URI.create' returns no validation code; ResourceType.URL/DATA constants exist but no check is applied to the scheme before rendering. I verified that XML escaping is applied (XMLWikiPrinter/XHTMLWriter via dom4j, and WikiPageUtil.escapeXmlString in wikimodel), so attribute breakout by quotes is not possible and the finding is specifically about the URI scheme, not about missing XML escaping. I verified the link-checker transformation and the HTML macro cleaning are unrelated paths (they do not validate link schemes either). I also checked that the untyped reference parsers route non-'://' strings to document/attachment/wiki references, so the URL-type path requires '://' (the 'javascript://%0a...' variant); the interwiki-fallback path does not have that restriction.
candidates.impact: Stored/DOM XSS in pages produced by the renderer: a user able to author content (without needing script or programming rights) can cause other users, including administrators, to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the wiki's origin when they activate the crafted link, enabling session/CSRF-token theft, actions with the victim's rights, and full compromise of the viewing account. The same unvalidated-scheme behaviour can be used for other dangerous URI schemes the embedding application does not expect (e.g. data: in additional contexts), and can defeat application-level expectations that the rendering layer emits only safe URL types.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The attacker can get markup rendered by the library for another user (any user with edit rights on wiki content, a comment, a message, or any consumer that renders untrusted syntax). 2) The victim activates the produced link (click) for the javascript: variant to execute. 3) For the interwiki variant, the attacker uses an alias that is not defined in RenderingConfiguration.getInterWikiDefinitions(); for the URL variant, the target must match the 'scheme://' pattern used by URLResourceReferenceTypeParser. 4) Counter-checks outside this snapshot: whether the consuming application (e.g. XWiki platform) applies an additional URL sanitizer to rendered output; nothing in this repository does so.
candidates.root_cause: The resource-reference layer types any string containing a 'scheme://' prefix as a URL without validating the scheme (URLResourceReferenceTypeParser.URL_SCHEME_PATTERN = "[a-zA-Z0-9+.-]*://"), and the XHTML link renderers then place the reference verbatim into the anchor's href attribute. XML-escaping is applied by the printer (so quotes cannot break out of the attribute), but the URI scheme is never restricted, so a scheme such as 'javascript:' is preserved into the produced markup. A second path reaches the same sink through interwiki references: when the interwiki alias is not present in the RenderingConfiguration definitions, InterWikiXHTMLLinkTypeRenderer falls back to writing the raw reference as the href. The XHTML parser has the same trust assumption: XWikiReferenceTagHandler.computeResourceReference maps an arbitrary href to ResourceType.URL (if it contains '://') or ResourceType.PATH otherwise, and the PATH/URL link type renderers write it back unchanged.
candidates.title: Link references with an unvalidated URI scheme (e.g. javascript:) are parsed and written verbatim into the rendered href attribute (XSS)
candidates.trace: Parse: GenericLinkReferenceParser.parse -> parseURILinks (lines 205-233): scheme = rawLink.substring(0, indexOf(':')); if the scheme is not in the allowed prefix list (only 'mailto' in the generic parser) the whole raw link is given to URLResourceReferenceTypeParser, whose regex '[a-zA-Z0-9+.-]*://' matches any scheme followed by '://' (line 59) -> ResourceReference(rawLink, ResourceType.URL) with typed=false. Interwiki alternative: parseInterWikiLinks (lines 241-251) splits on the last non-escaped '@' and builds an InterWikiResourceReference whose reference is everything before the alias. Render: XHTMLChainingRenderer.beginLink (lines 248-262) delegates to XHTMLLinkRenderer; DefaultXHTMLLinkTypeRenderer.beginLinkExtraAttributes (line 44) puts reference.getReference() into the anchorAttributes map under HREF; InterWikiXHTMLLinkTypeRenderer (lines 59-64) uses the configured interwiki URL if the alias is defined, otherwise the raw reference. AbstractXHTMLLinkTypeRenderer.beginLink (lines 139-162) passes these attributes to XHTMLWikiPrinter.printXMLStartElement, which produces <a href="<reference>">. The reference is XML-entity-escaped (quotes/angle brackets), but the scheme is untouched, so 'javascript:alert(1)' and 'javascript://%0aalert(1)' survive as executable URL schemes. The same sink is reachable in the XHTML-parsing direction: XWikiReferenceTagHandler.computeResourceReference (lines 181-199) classifies an arbitrary href as URL (contains '://') or PATH (everything else); PathXHTMLLinkTypeRenderer inherits the default href write, so 'javascript:...' re-renders unchanged.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-verified (no tests or execution allowed in this review). Whether the embedding application (XWiki platform, which is not part of this snapshot) adds an output HTML/URL sanitizer that strips javascript: hrefs is unknown; if such a sanitizer exists downstream, impact is reduced. Whether the javascript:// URL form is executed by all supported browsers was not verified here. Also unknown whether some consumers consider raw URI pass-through intentional (the renderer's javadoc does not guarantee any scheme filtering).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 / CWE-83: Improper neutralization of user-controlled URI scheme in generated link attribute (XSS via javascript: URL)

coverage_summary: Source scope reported by get_source_scope: 764 model-visible files (763 indexed by the P1 index, 1 source file missing from the index, 2 parse errors, source_file_hash_mismatches 0, no sensitive-name/symlink exclusions, 5 MiB per-file text limit, binary-like files refused). Modules reviewed: xwiki-rendering-api (blocks, listeners/chaining, parser reference/type parsers, renderers, syntax, transformations core), xwiki-rendering-xml (XMLWikiPrinter/XHTMLWikiPrinter/XHTMLWriter/SAXSerializer), xwiki-rendering-wikimodel (xrefs to XhtmlParser/TagStack/MacroInfo/WikiPageUtil/LocalEntityResolver), xwiki-rendering-syntaxes (xhtml, xhtml5, html5, annotatedxhtml, annotatedhtml5, xwiki20, xwiki21, xdomxml10/current, plain, event, doxia, docbook, apt, creole, jspwiki, twiki, wikimodel bridge), xwiki-rendering-macros (html, raw, content, box, message, figure, footnotes, id, toc, comment, ctsreport), xwiki-rendering-transformations (macro, icon, wikiword, linkchecker), xwiki-rendering-legacy, xwiki-rendering-test resources and poms. I did not review every method of every file line-by-line; the poms, resource bundles, cts test data and smaller unexamined classes (e.g. full Doxia XWikiGeneratorSink, full TagStack, most block classes) were skimmed or sampled. Per the P1 relation scope, the index provides syntax containment plus name/type/arity call and inheritance candidates only: control flow, data flow and semantic resolution are not implemented, so no indexed edge was treated as proof of reachability, and files not present in the index were not assumed clean. No code was executed and no build/tests/scanners were run.
limitations: No runtime confirmation is possible in this review: the candidate is a static lead only, and no exploit was executed.
The repository snapshot contains no test sources, so upstream expected behaviour (e.g. escaping/validation tests that would normally pin the safe behaviour) could not be consulted.
The consuming application (XWiki platform) is not part of the snapshot; any downstream HTML sanitizer or output filter for rendered content is unknown and could neutralize or confirm the candidate.

The P1 relation index is partial (37 parsed Java files of 602, 5723 unresolved calls, no control-flow/data-flow/semantic resolution); it was used only for navigation and every checked edge was verified in source text.

Dependency behaviour that the code relies on (xwiki-commons-xml HTMLCleaner restricted/default modes, LocalEntityResolver, dom4j XMLWriter escaping, jsoup/HTML5 parsing) is outside the assigned sources and was not inspected.

Large/complex files (DefaultXWikiGeneratorListener ~35 KB, XWikiSyntaxChainingRenderer ~33 KB, XWikiGeneratorSink ~23 KB, TagStack ~15 KB) were reviewed selectively rather than exhaustively, so an additional defect in unread regions cannot be excluded.
The rejected leads (link-checker SSRF, XHTML comment/metadata round-trip injection, ContentMacro+syntax cleaning bypass) remain unconfirmed rather than disproven.

rejected_leads.lead: Blind SSRF in the link checked transformation: LinkCheckerTransformation enqueues every LinkBlock whose ResourceType is URL, DefaultLinkCheckerThread.checkLink calls DefaultHTTPChecker.check(url) which does new HttpGet(url) + httpClient.execute with no host/IP allow-list or deny-list (DefaultHTTPChecker.java lines 86-113; LinkCheckerTransformation.java lines 105-123; DefaultLinkCheckerThread.java lines 197-219).
rejected_leads.reason: The behaviour is the documented purpose of the transformation ('Looks for external URLs in links and verify their status'), the response body is not returned to the attacker (blind, only status code/events), and in XWiki this transformation must be enabled explicitly (it is not in the default transformation list). I could not establish that the missing network restrictions are treated as a defect in this version, so it is a weaker lead than the href/scheme issue.

rejected_leads.lead: Comment/metadata-driven XHTML round-trip injection: XWikiCommentHandler.onComment interprets '<!--startmacro: ... -->' / 'startwikilink' / 'startimage' comments and XHTMLXWikiGeneratorListener.createMetaData turns any data-xwiki-* attribute (and class="xwiki-metadata-container") into XDOM metadata, so HTML comments/attributes that survive cleaning could inject macros, links or non-generated-content metadata when content is parsed back (WYSIWYG/annotated XHTML round trip), potentially executing macros with the editing user's rights.
rejected_leads.reason: This parser protocol is intentional (it is how annotated XHTML and the editor round-trip work), and I could not demonstrate within this snapshot that the surrounding platform (HTML cleaner behaviour, editor save path, rights checks on the injected macro) allows the injected markup to survive to the point of execution. Evidence for concrete exploitability is outside this repository, so I did not report it as a candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: ContentMacro can parse unprivileged content with an HTML/XHTML syntax via its user-chosen 'syntax' parameter (ContentMacro.java lines 92-106), which uses HTMLParser/HTML5Parser with the default (non-RESTRICTED) HTMLCleaner configuration, bypassing the HTML macro's restricted cleaning; blocks are then rendered, and any raw text becomes a RawBlock.
rejected_leads.reason: The dangerous step depends on the behaviour of xwiki-commons-xml HTMLCleaner (not part of this snapshot): if the default configuration already strips script/event handlers, the path is not exploitable, and in XWiki the printer's HTMLElementSanitizer adds a second filter. I could not verify cleaner behaviour from the assigned sources, so this remains unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: HTMLRawBlockFilter condition uses '(HTML_FAMILY_TYPES.contains(...) && parameters.isClean()) || restricted' (HTMLRawBlockFilter.java lines 76-78), a suspicious operator precedence that also runs the HTML cleaner for non-HTML syntaxes in restricted contexts.
rejected_leads.reason: This makes cleaning broader, not weaker (no bypass): in restricted contexts cleaning always happens with RESTRICTED=true; without restriction, clean=true still triggers cleaning for HTML-family raw blocks. The oddity appears to be upstream code style, not a security hole.

rejected_leads.lead: XHTMLWriter.escapeAttributeEntities replaces ''' with '&' (XHTMLWriter.java lines 57-61), which looks like a wrong numeric entity (should be ').
rejected_leads.reason: With dom4j's default attribute quote character ('"'), apostrophes are not escaped at all, so the replacement is effectively dead code; the observable effect would be data corruption, not injection. Kept as an observation only.

summary: Repo: xwiki-rendering (parent pom version 14.10.3, tag xwiki-rendering-14.10.3), a rendering library that turns wiki/HTML/XHTML input into XHTML/HTML5 output. I reviewed the API module (block/listener/parser/reference/transformation), the syntax modules (xhtml, xhtml5, html5, xwiki20/xwiki21, annotated/xhtml, annotated/html5, xdomxml10, plain/event/doxia parsers), the macros and the transformation modules, focusing on attacker-controlled input reaching output, escaping/cleaning code, privilege/restricted-context propagation, network sinks and parser trust boundaries. Most security-critical machinery I could compare against expected behaviour is present and coherent (XWikiSyntaxEscapeHandler escaping, XHTMLWikiPrinter {{/html}} and '{' encoding, XHTMLWriter, HTMLRawBlockFilter restricted cleaning + HTMLCleanerConfiguration.RESTRICTED, DefaultMacroContentParser restricted propagation, noopener addition for target=_blank, xml escaping in XMLWikiPrinter, secure XML parsing). One issue stood out as the strongest attacker-controlled input path with a concrete security impact: link references are accepted with an arbitrary URI scheme and emitted verbatim into the href attribute of the generated anchor, with no scheme/allow-list validation anywhere in the repository. I submit that as the single candidate (a lead, not confirmed at runtime). I also recorded the other plausible leads I could not substantiate (link-checker SSRF, HTML-comment driven XHTML round-trip injection, ContentMacro+HTML-parser bypass) as rejected/unconfirmed.
